Kageaki"Subaru ji. No. She woke a little while ago. I thought my sitting beside her might disturb her rest."
Subaru"Achha, good. Not started creating havoc, has she?"

Subaru"You are satisfied with that?"
Kageaki"Yes."
Subaru"Then do that."

To give my awkwardness somewhere to go, I looked at a pillar for no reason. A sound choice. A pillar did not require conversation. It had its work, holding the house up; I had mine, appearing to have a reason for looking at it. Between us, a very satisfactory silence.

Only the woman in the bed had not joined this arrangement. From the corner of my eye I checked—◆she was watching me.

Steadily.
Straight at me.

The right cheek receiving this attention had become strangely hot. Achha. The pillar was doing nothing to help. Entire roof it could support, but one embarrassed man was beyond its capacity.

I had said my part. Now I shut my mouth and watched her without even blinking. Hesitation moved in her eyes.

In practical terms, the proposal should give little trouble. For the town, a minus became a plus: no more plunder, and the fields producing again. An excellent exchange. Enough to let bygones be bygones—probably.

For the masterless warriors who had become bandits, likewise. Surely they were not so optimistic as to think this life could continue forever. Once matters at the center settled, the shogunate would turn its attention to order in the provinces.

At the end of their present road waited execution as criminals. Put down their weapons and join the town, and they could avoid that end.

No difficulty.

...So, if even then she could not accept—

It had to be done.
Just as last night I had refused him as a samurai.

As a samurai.

Achha. What was a samurai?
Someone who ruled the people by armed force.

Rule by force. Protect by force. Take by force.
Three activities, one instrument. No confusion in the profession.

Not, under any circumstances,
someone living on the people's kindness.

Last night he had offered us fields. Live there, he had said.

Mercy.
Goodwill.

That was why I could not accept. A samurai did not lean on the generosity of the people. Talwar meri, roti tumhaari? My sword, your charity? What kind of arrangement was this? The sword would have to look away while I ate.

Plunder, be hated, despised, condemned: that life I could accept. The lowest, meanest way of being a samurai, but still inside the boundary.

Haan. Rob the people, and my standing survived. Accept something freely given, and my standing died. Such was the boundary. It did not become less real because somebody could laugh at it.

A bandit could remain a samurai.
Take his offered hand, though, and I would no longer be one.

No longer a samurai.

en.html:
No cleverness. Simply asking.
Bowed flat, begging.

What else could I do? The argument had already reached its conclusion. Very fine argument. It had arrived at the destination, locked the door and left me outside.

I had failed to reconcile the town's interests with theirs. Interest and advantage alone did not move them.

They were samurai.
Their foundation was force.

If they insisted on remaining samurai here, what was left but the mountain and banditry? Expelled from the regular army, they had no other way.

The conclusion was there.
So I asked.

Please. Bas, please. No secret fourth answer hidden under my forehead. I put that forehead on the ground anyway.

When the reasoning would not permit something and I still wanted it, asking was all that remained.

Bend your principle.
Give up being samurai.
